Newmont stock faces higher 2027 costs as Penasquito output falls
sum: Newmont expects its 2026 gold-production costs to finish below the plan set at the start of the year, but the outlook becomes more demanding in 2027 as silver output at Penasquito declines. The cost and cash-flow picture was outlined in a Trefis analysis published by Yahoo Finance on Friday, November 13.

Newmont now expects 2026 all-in sustaining costs of 1,520 US dollars per ounce of gold, according to the analysis. That is about 10 percent below the guidance issued at the beginning of the year. Higher prices for copper, silver and other co-products, together with cost discipline, are supporting the improvement.

The company produced 11 million ounces of silver in the third quarter, with quarterly all-in sustaining costs of 1,450 US dollars per ounce after by-product credits. For the fourth quarter, management expects costs of about 1,900 US dollars per ounce, the highest level of 2026, partly because Penasquito silver production is expected to fall to about half its third-quarter level.

The same mine-sequencing effect is expected to continue into 2027, when Penasquito silver output is projected to be roughly 30 percent below 2026 levels. That could reduce the contribution from by-product credits and leave Newmont more exposed to gold prices and operating-cost execution. The next all-in sustaining cost update is expected with the February 2027 report.

Newmont returned about 1.9 billion US dollars through dividends and share repurchases between its second- and third-quarter calls. Management also said the company had bought back more than 115 million shares, equivalent to about 10 percent of shares outstanding, since February 2024.

Free cash flow rose to 1.91 billion US dollars in the third quarter from 1.57 billion US dollars a year earlier. The analysis cautions that higher gold prices helped the latest profit, so strong cash generation does not by itself remove the risk of higher unit costs when silver volumes decline.

Newmont (NEM) digs up silver and copper alongside its gold, and those metals may matter more to the stock than most investors think. You probably see Newmont as a bet on the gold price, yet the stock trades at 13.4 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. The price appears to doubt that today’s profit lasts. But Newmont’s profit also comes from what each ounce costs to produce, not only from what gold sells for. So how much lower are Newmont’s gold costs running than it planned?

Silver is not a sideline. Newmont produced 11 million ounces of silver in the third quarter. Its all-in sustaining cost that quarter was $1,450 per ounce, with by-products counted as a credit. Management said unit costs improved from the second quarter on higher gold and co-product volumes. So for 2026, silver and copper are helping to lower what Newmont’s gold costs.

Most of it is going back to shareholders. Newmont returned about $1.9 billion through its dividend and buybacks between its second-quarter and third-quarter calls. Management said the company has bought back more than 115 million shares, about 10% of shares outstanding, since February 2024, and the diluted share count fell to 1,051 million in the quarter ended September 30, 2026, from 1,100 million a year earlier.

The cash behind those returns is growing. Free cash flow was $1.91 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, up from $1.57 billion a year earlier. Management said the quarter’s operating performance translated into that cash.
Yet the cash does not fully settle whether today’s profit can last. Newmont’s third-quarter profit beat estimates on higher gold prices, so not all of that cash comes from lower costs.

Less silver. Management expects fourth-quarter all-in sustaining costs of about $1,900 per ounce, the highest of the year. This is partly because silver output at Penasquito falls to about half its third-quarter level. For 2027, the company expects unit costs to trend higher, with silver at Penasquito roughly 30% below 2026 levels because of planned mine sequencing.

sum: Goldman Sachs is sticking with its "Buy" rating on Newmont, and the reasoning behind that call rests on two pillars: a quarterly profit that cleared Wall Street's bar and a hefty slug of free cash. The complication is timing. Just as the gold miner's numbers impress, management is flagging a steeper cost path through the end of the year and beyond.

The headline beat was decisive. Newmont posted adjusted earnings of $2.20 per share for the third quarter of 2026, comfortably ahead of the $1.94 consensus. Adjusted net income came in at $2.3 billion. Goldman Sachs counts the major gold producers among the more defensive names in the sector, and on that basis keeps Newmont on its buy list.

Cash generation is where the case gains real weight. Free cash flow for the quarter reached $1.9 billion, while operating cash flow hit $2.8 billion. By the end of September, the company held $8.8 billion in liquid funds—a war chest that underpins both shareholder returns and future projects. Since its last earnings call, Newmont has already returned money to investors through dividends and share buybacks.

External conditions have been cooperating. Reuters reported on Thursday that gold prices rose following the US midterm elections, helped by a weaker dollar, lower Treasury yields and easing fears of oil-driven inflation. Newmont was among the gold miners whose shares advanced on the move. A 1.9% gain on Friday extended that friendly run.
Yet a favorable market tide only carries real quality when it meets operational delivery—and that is precisely where the cost question bites.

About two weeks ago, Newmont lowered its full-year guidance for all-in sustaining costs (AISC) per gold ounce to roughly $1,520, down from $1,680. In the quarter just reported, those costs came in at $1,454 an ounce. That improved outlook forms the positive backdrop to Goldman's endorsement.
The forward path, however, demands attention. For the fourth quarter of 2026, Newmont expects AISC of about $1,900 per ounce, and unit costs are projected to rise again in 2027.

sum: Shares in Newmont Corporation (NEM +9.87%) rose 34.5% in August, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The move comes amid rising gold prices and positive news on the administrative and operational fronts regarding the resolution of a dispute with Barrick Mining Corporation (B +8.30%). In addition, I would argue that the appeal of gold as a safe-haven investment increased throughout the month.

The price of gold rose throughout the month, and given the operational leverage miners have to commodity prices, it's not surprising that the market bought up the stock and took it sharply higher in August.

Still, the increase in gold prices is not a stock-specific issue, as many other gold miners would have benefited as well. The main operational and administrative plus for the month came from the agreement with Barrick Mining regarding their Nevada Gold Mines joint venture, announced on Aug. 10.

The two companies agreed that Newmont would pay Barrick $1.95 billion to include certain Barrick assets in the joint venture. Furthermore, Newmont consented to Barrick's intended initial public offering (IPO) of its North American gold assets. The resolution of the dispute helps Barrick achieve its strategic objectives and derisks Newmont's stock as well. It also allows the joint venture to generate operational synergies by adding the new assets, thereby increasing the value of Newmont's 38.5% stake.

Turning to the more contentious part of the argument, the persistently high U.S. government bond yields through the month are arguably one reason why gold and gold mining stocks have come into favor. Historically speaking, rising bond yields are bad for gold because the yield on a safe asset (U.S. debt) rises relative to gold's yield, which is zero.

However, what if rising U.S. government yields are due to increasing skepticism over government debt levels? It's a legitimate question given that U.S. public debt topped $40 trillion this month and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is actively intervening in the markets to try to reduce U.S. Treasury yields. Moreover, continued geopolitical conflict may well cause global central banks to prefer holding gold over U.S. Treasuries -- a long-term trend that supports the price of gold.

sum: Shares of Newmont Mining (NEM +9.90%) rallied on Wednesday, up 7.9% for the day.

Newmont already reported second-quarter earnings in late July, and there wasn't much company-specific news today. Newmont did announce it had agreed to sell an undeveloped gold project to Canadian mining company StrikePoint Gold for $70 million, plus an additional $50 million contingent payment tied to future milestones.

However, for the world's largest mining company that primarily mines gold, that small divestiture is relatively inconsequential. More consequential was today's rise in gold prices, driven by lower long-term interest rates, which appeared to be due to an increase in the Treasury Department's Treasury Bond buyback program announced this morning.

In recent days, the yields on longer-dated Treasury Bonds have increased to multi-decade highs. All else equal, higher long-term yields reduce the value of future earnings and have also tended to reduce the value of assets that don't pay cash interest or dividends.
Gold fits into this category, as gold tends to be seen as a store of value against inflation, but it's not an asset that pays out cash to its owners.

This morning, the U.S. Treasury Department under Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced at least a doubling of its Treasury Bond buyback program for long-dated Treasuries. The signal the Treasury is sending is that it will likely buy back longer-dated Treasuries at a discount, since long-term rates have risen, in an effort to tamp down longer-term interest rates. The Treasury Department will likely sell shorter-term Treasury bills and notes to do so.

That may put the Treasury at greater risk of short-term inflationary spikes, but the announcement did result in declining yields on longer-term Treasury Bonds today. And lower yields on long-term bonds tend to be a positive for gold prices.

sum: On 10 November, Justice Colvin of the Federal Court of Australia delivered judgment in Newmont v Commissioner of Taxation. The proceedings have been on foot since 2017.

The 3-week case heard in August 2024 concerned Newmont’s liability to tax on aggregate capital gains of approximately $320 million resulting from a restructure of the holding of its Australian gold mining assets including the Boddington Mine in WA in 2011.
The principal issue was whether Division 855 (TARP or “taxable Australian real property”) applied to “disregard” the gains for Australian tax purposes.
The Court has not made final orders. It will do so after several issues are reported on by a referee.
The decision addresses a number of issues of potentially wide import in the context of the Div 855 “TARP” regime, including:
- The meaning of “real property” in the context of Div 855 (see also the recent YTL decision)
- The approach to valuing particular assets (or allocating value to assets) in the context of the TARP regime
